# 2 Maccabees Chapter 3 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 3 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_003_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 3 is one of the most dramatically realized miracle narratives in the deuterocanon. The three agents show significant divergence in the register of the theophany (vv. 22–28), the description of the angelic attackers, and Heliodorus's final testimony. PNEUMA consistently dramatizes; EMET maintains formal distance; LOGOS balances these impulses. The SOPHIA consensus preserves the drama while maintaining translational precision.

---

**1** While the holy city was at complete peace and the laws were being upheld faithfully because of the piety of the high priest Onias and his hatred of wickedness,

**2** it came about that the kings themselves honored the place and glorified the temple with magnificent gifts.

**3** King Seleucus of Asia defrayed from his own revenues all the expenses pertaining to the service of the sacrifices.

**4** But a man named Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed administrator of the temple, had a dispute with the high priest Onias about the regulation of the city market.

**5** When he could not prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,

**6** and reported that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of untold sums of money, so large as to be beyond all counting, and that these funds did not belong to the sacrificial account but could come under the power of the king.

**7** When Apollonius had an audience with the king, he informed him of the money that had been reported to him. The king selected Heliodorus, his chief minister, and sent him with orders to remove those funds.

**8** Heliodorus set out at once, using as his official cover a tour of inspection through the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but actually intending to carry out the king's design.

**9** When he arrived in Jerusalem and had been received with courtesy by the high priest of the city, he told him what had been reported and revealed the purpose for which he had come, and he inquired whether this was indeed the case.

**10** The high priest explained that these were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,

**11** and that some funds also belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very prominent standing. The total came to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. He declared that it was utterly impossible to wrong those who had put their trust in the holiness of the place and in the dignity and inviolability of this temple, honored throughout the whole world.

**12** But Heliodorus insisted that in any case, by the king's orders, these funds must be confiscated for the royal treasury.

**13** So he set a date and went in to conduct the inspection. There was no small distress throughout the whole city.

**14** The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their priestly vestments and called out to heaven upon him who had given the law concerning deposits, begging that he keep the funds safe for those who had entrusted them.

**15** To see the face of the high priest was to be wounded at heart, for his appearance and the change of his color disclosed the anguish of his soul.

**16** Terror and trembling of the body had come over the man, which made plain to all who looked at him the depth of pain lodged in his heart.

**17** People rushed out of their houses in crowds to make a common supplication, because the holy place was about to be brought into dishonor.

**18** Women girded with sackcloth under their breasts thronged the streets. Young women who had been kept indoors ran together — some to the gates, some to the walls, while others peered out of the windows.

**19** All of them stretched their hands toward heaven in supplication.

**20** There was something pitiable in the prostration of the whole multitude and the anguish of the high priest in his great distress.

**21** While they were all calling upon the almighty LORD to keep safe what had been entrusted, for those who had entrusted it, Heliodorus pressed on with his purpose.

**22** But just as Heliodorus arrived at the treasury with his bodyguard, the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority caused so great a manifestation that all who had dared to accompany him were struck down by the power of God and overcome with terror.

**23** For there appeared to them a horse with a terrifying rider, adorned with magnificent trappings. It rushed forward violently and struck Heliodorus with its front hooves. Its rider appeared to be clothed in golden armor.

**24** Two young men also appeared, exceedingly strong and surpassingly beautiful, with glory surrounding them. They stood on either side of Heliodorus and flogged him continuously, delivering blow after blow.

**25** Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground, overwhelmed by great darkness. His men picked him up and placed him on a stretcher,

**26** and carried him away — this man who had entered the treasury moments before with a great retinue and all his bodyguard, but was now utterly unable to help himself. They acknowledged clearly the sovereign power of God.

**27** While he lay prostrate, speechless from the divine intervention and without any hope of recovery,

**28** they praised the LORD who had worked such wonders for his own holy place. And the temple, which had been filled with fear and disturbance a little while before, was filled with joy and gladness, because the almighty LORD had appeared.

**29** Some of Heliodorus's companions quickly besought Onias to call upon the Most High to grant life to the man who lay at the very point of death.

**30** The high priest, fearing that the king might suspect the Jews of foul play in the matter of Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the man's recovery.

**31** While the high priest was making the propitiatory sacrifice, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus, dressed in the same garments. They stood over him and said: "Give great thanks to the high priest Onias, for it is for his sake that the LORD has granted you your life.

**32** And you yourself, having been scourged from heaven, declare to all people the majestic power of God." Having said this, they vanished.

**33** So Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made very great vows to the Savior of his life. He bade farewell to Onias and marched back with his forces to the king.

**34** He bore testimony before all people to the works of the supreme God, which he had witnessed with his own eyes.

**35** When the king asked Heliodorus what sort of person would be suitable to send to Jerusalem again, he replied:

**36** "If you have an enemy or a plotter against the government, send him there, and you will receive him back well flogged — if indeed he escapes with his life at all — for there is truly some divine power in that place.

**37** For he who has his dwelling in heaven watches over that place himself, brings it aid, and strikes down and destroys those who come to do it harm."

**38** Thus the affair of Heliodorus and the preservation of the treasury came to this end.

---

## Translator's Notes

- **v. 4, "tribe of Benjamin"**: Some manuscripts read "Bilgah" — possibly a priestly course name. "Benjamin" is the reading of Codex Alexandrinus.
- **v. 22, "Sovereign of spirits"**: Greek *ho tōn pneumatōn kai pasēs exousias dynastēs* — Lord of spirits and all authority. A remarkable title appearing here and in later Jewish apocalyptic literature (cf. 1 Enoch). SOPHIA preserves "Sovereign."
- **vv. 23–24, the angelic horseman**: The description follows Hellenistic epiphany conventions (the divine warrior on horseback). The two young men (*neaniai*) flanking Heliodorus recall similar figures in 2 Maccabees 11:8 and other apocalyptic texts.
- **v. 30, propitiatory sacrifice**: The theology here is significant — the high priest intercedes for a pagan enemy. This models an ethic of intercession that transcends ethnic and religious boundaries.
- **v. 36, Heliodorus's testimony**: The narrative closes with a Gentile king's minister attesting the reality of Israel's God. This is a classic apologetic pattern in Hellenistic Jewish literature (cf. Tobit, Judith).
